title: Result modelling
summary: When failure is a normal outcome, return it as a value instead of throwing.

steps.title: Not every failure is exceptional
body: A customer types `abc` into a quantity box. A promo code has expired. A search finds nobody called Maya.
None of these is a surprise. They happen all day, and your program has a planned response to each. Using exceptions for them has real costs:
- **They are invisible.** Nothing in `decimal Withdraw(decimal amount)` warns the caller it might throw. People forget the `try`.
- **They jump.** The reader has to work out where control lands.
- **They stop at the first problem.** A form with three mistakes reports one.
| A bug, or the world is broken: null where it is forbidden, disk full, corrupt file | **throw** |
| An outcome you expect and the caller must handle: bad input, not found, not allowed | **return** it |
When failure is part of the method's job description, put it in the return type. Then the compiler makes every caller look at it.

steps.prompt: Throw an exception, or return the failure as a value?
items: A method is passed `null` for an argument that must never be null
The program's own data file is corrupt
A loop index runs past the end of an array because of a bug
A customer types letters into the quantity box
A search finds no customer with that name
steps.explain: The first three mean the program or its surroundings are broken, and no caller has a sensible plan for them. The last three are everyday outcomes that the caller is expected to deal with.

steps.title: The Try pattern
body: You have already met the simplest way to return a failure. `int.TryParse` returns a `bool` for *did it work*, and hands back the value through an `out` parameter.
No exception, no `try`, and the caller cannot get at `quantity` without tripping over the `bool` first.
You can write your own in the same style. The conventions: the name starts with `Try`, it returns `bool`, and when it returns `false` the `out` value is set to a harmless default.
bool TryGetDiscount(string code, out int percent)
`Dictionary.TryGetValue` works the same way. It is the standard shape for *this might not be there*.

code: bool ok = int.TryParse("4x", out int b);
steps.explain: The first parse works, so `a` is 42. The second fails: `TryParse` returns `false` and sets the `out` value to 0. Nothing is thrown.

steps.title: TryParseQuantity
prompt: Two lessons ago you parsed a quantity with `try` and `catch`. Do it properly now.
Write `bool TryParseQuantity(string text, out int quantity)`.
- returns `true` and sets `quantity` when `text` is a whole number from **1 to 99**
- otherwise returns `false` and sets `quantity` to `0`
```csharp
TryParseQuantity("12", out int q);    // true,  q is 12
TryParseQuantity("500", out int q);   // false, q is 0
No exceptions in either direction.
starter: bool TryParseQuantity(string text, out int quantity)
solution: bool TryParseQuantity(string text, out int quantity)
if (int.TryParse(text, out int parsed) && parsed >= 1 && parsed <= 99)
template: {{CODE}}
bool dojoOk = TryParseQuantity("12", out int dojoQ);
Dojo.Eq("\"12\" returns true", true, dojoOk);
Dojo.Eq("...and quantity is 12", 12, dojoQ);
Dojo.Eq("\"1\" returns true", true, TryParseQuantity("1", out dojoQ));
Dojo.Eq("\"99\" returns true", true, TryParseQuantity("99", out dojoQ));
Dojo.Eq("...and quantity is 99", 99, dojoQ);
Dojo.Eq("\"abc\" returns false", false, TryParseQuantity("abc", out dojoQ));
Dojo.Eq("...and quantity is 0", 0, dojoQ);
Dojo.Eq("\"0\" returns false", false, TryParseQuantity("0", out dojoQ));
Dojo.Eq("\"500\" returns false", false, TryParseQuantity("500", out dojoQ));
Dojo.Eq("...and quantity is 0, not 500", 0, dojoQ);
Dojo.Eq("\"-3\" returns false", false, TryParseQuantity("-3", out dojoQ));
Dojo.Eq("\"\" returns false", false, TryParseQuantity("", out dojoQ));
hints: Build on `int.TryParse(text, out int parsed)`. Parse into a separate variable so a rejected number such as 500 never reaches `quantity`.
Success needs three things to be true: it parsed, `parsed >= 1`, and `parsed <= 99`.
On success: `quantity = parsed; return true;`. In every other case: `quantity = 0; return false;`

steps.title: A Result that says why
body: `bool` tells the caller *that* it failed. Often they need to know **why**, to show the customer a message. So return a small object that is either a success with a value, or a failure with a reason.

Here is one. You will be **given** this type in the exercises, so read it rather than memorise it. `Result<T>` is read *result of T*, and `T` is whatever type the success value has, just like `List<T>`.
private Result(bool isSuccess, T? value, string error) { ... }
public static Result<T> Ok(T value)       => new Result<T>(true, value, "");
public static Result<T> Fail(string error) => new Result<T>(false, default, error);
The constructor is private. The only ways in are `Ok` and `Fail`, so a result is never both or neither. Using it:
Now the signature is honest: this returns a decimal, **or a reason why not**.

steps.prompt: Complete the method so that it reports both kinds of failure and one success.
steps.explain: `Fail` takes the reason as text. `Ok` takes the value. The types stop you mixing them up: `Ok` will not accept a string here, and `Fail` will not accept a number.

steps.prompt: `var result = Withdraw(50m, 80m);` has just run. How should the caller use it?
options: Check `result.IsSuccess`; read `result.Value` if it is true, otherwise show `result.Error`
Read `result.Value` straight away; it will be 0 if anything went wrong
Wrap the call in `try` and `catch`, because `Fail` throws
steps.explain: A failed result still has a `Value`, but it is only a meaningless default. `IsSuccess` is the question to ask first. Nothing here throws, and `Withdraw` never returns null.

steps.title: Validation: collect every error
body: Sign-up forms are where exceptions fit worst. The user got three fields wrong. An exception reports the first, they fix it, submit, and meet the second. Nobody enjoys that.
Validation should return **all** the problems at once. The simplest shape is a list of messages, where an empty list means valid.
Notice the checks are separate `if`s, not `else if`. Each rule gets its say.
The caller decides what to do: `errors.Count == 0` means carry on. Otherwise show them, perhaps joined into one line with `string.Join("; ", errors)`.

steps.prompt: Build a validator that reports every problem. Check the name before the age.
steps.explain: Create the list, let each rule add to it, and return it at the end. An empty list means everything passed.

steps.prompt: Match each way of reporting failure to what the caller gets.
pairs: yes or no, plus the value on success
a value, or one reason why not
a jump out of the method, for bugs and breakages
nothing was found, with no reason given

steps.title: Sign-up without exceptions
prompt: Write three methods for a sign-up form. `Result<T>` from the card is **already provided**: use `Result<int>.Ok(...)`, `Result<int>.Fail(...)`, `.IsSuccess`, `.Value` and `.Error`.
**`Result<int> ParseAge(string text)`**
- not a whole number: fail with `"Age must be a number"`
- below 0 or above 130: fail with `"Age must be between 0 and 130"`
- otherwise succeed with the age
**`List<string> ValidateSignup(string name, string email, string ageText)`** returns **every** problem, in this order:
- `"Name is required"` when the name is empty or only spaces
- `"Email must contain @"` when it does not
- the error from `ParseAge`, when it fails
**`Result<string> Register(string name, string email, string ageText)`**
- with no errors: succeed with `"Welcome, Maya"` (using the name)
- otherwise: fail with all the errors joined by `"; "`
Nothing here should throw or catch.
starter: return Result<int>.Fail("Age must be a number");
List<string> ValidateSignup(string name, string email, string ageText)
Result<string> Register(string name, string email, string ageText)
solution: return Result<int>.Fail("Age must be a number");
return Result<int>.Fail("Age must be between 0 and 130");
List<string> ValidateSignup(string name, string email, string ageText)
Result<string> Register(string name, string email, string ageText)
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("ParseAge(\"34\") succeeds", true, ParseAge("34").IsSuccess);
Dojo.Eq("...with the value 34", 34, ParseAge("34").Value);
Dojo.Eq("ParseAge(\"0\") and ParseAge(\"130\") succeed", true, ParseAge("0").IsSuccess && ParseAge("130").IsSuccess);
Dojo.Eq("ParseAge(\"old\") fails", false, ParseAge("old").IsSuccess);
Dojo.Eq("...with: Age must be a number", "Age must be a number", ParseAge("old").Error);
Dojo.Eq("ParseAge(\"131\") fails with the range message", "Age must be between 0 and 130", ParseAge("131").Error);
Dojo.Eq("ParseAge(\"-1\") fails with the range message", "Age must be between 0 and 130", ParseAge("-1").Error);
Dojo.Eq("a valid sign-up has no errors", new List<string>(), ValidateSignup("Maya", "maya@example.com", "34"));
Dojo.Eq("a blank name is reported", new List<string> { "Name is required" }, ValidateSignup("  ", "maya@example.com", "34"));
Dojo.Eq("a bad email is reported", new List<string> { "Email must contain @" }, ValidateSignup("Maya", "maya.example.com", "34"));
Dojo.Eq("a bad age is reported using ParseAge's message", new List<string> { "Age must be between 0 and 130" }, ValidateSignup("Maya", "maya@example.com", "200"));
Dojo.Eq("three mistakes give three errors, in order", new List<string> { "Name is required", "Email must contain @", "Age must be a number" }, ValidateSignup("", "nope", "old"));
Dojo.Eq("Register succeeds for valid input", true, Register("Maya", "maya@example.com", "34").IsSuccess);
Dojo.Eq<string?>("...with the value: Welcome, Maya", "Welcome, Maya", Register("Maya", "maya@example.com", "34").Value);
Dojo.Eq("Register fails when anything is wrong", false, Register("Maya", "nope", "34").IsSuccess);
Dojo.Eq("...with the one error", "Email must contain @", Register("Maya", "nope", "34").Error);
Dojo.Eq("Register joins several errors with \"; \"", "Name is required; Age must be a number", Register("", "a@b.c", "x").Error);
class Result<T>
public bool IsSuccess { get; }
public T? Value { get; }
public string Error { get; }
private Result(bool isSuccess, T? value, string error) { IsSuccess = isSuccess; Value = value; Error = error; }
public static Result<T> Ok(T value) => new Result<T>(true, value, "");
public static Result<T> Fail(string error) => new Result<T>(false, default, error);
hints: `ParseAge` starts with `if (!int.TryParse(text, out int age)) return Result<int>.Fail("Age must be a number");`, then checks the range, then returns `Result<int>.Ok(age)`.
In `ValidateSignup`, call `ParseAge(ageText)` and, if `!result.IsSuccess`, add `result.Error` to the list. That way the age rules live in one place.
`Register` calls `ValidateSignup`. If `errors.Count > 0`, return `Result<string>.Fail(string.Join("; ", errors))`. Otherwise return `Result<string>.Ok($"Welcome, {name}")`.
